case_summary: The case involves a dispute among the legal heirs of the original partners of a partnership firm 'Soorajmull Nagarmull' constituted in 1943. The plaintiffs, heirs of some deceased partners, filed a suit seeking declarations of entitlement to the firm's assets and properties, rights to represent the firm, injunctions against defendants representing the firm, disclosure of accounts, and dissolution of the firm. The defendants challenged the suit's maintainability and sought its dismissal on grounds including lack of cause of action and limitation.
legal_issues: Whether the plaintiffs, as legal heirs of deceased partners, have a cause of action to claim ownership and rights over the partnership firm's assets and properties.
Whether the plaintiffs are entitled to seek dissolution of the partnership firm and winding up of its affairs.
Whether the plaint discloses a cause of action under Order VII Rule 11 CPC warranting rejection at the threshold.
Whether the suit is maintainable given the provisions of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 and the terms of the Partnership Deed.
court_reasoning: The Supreme Court agreed with the Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court that the plaintiffs, being legal heirs and not partners themselves, do not have any right, title, or interest in the assets and properties of the firm while it is carrying on business. The Court noted that under the Indian Partnership Act, only partners can seek dissolution of the firm, and the partnership deed specifically provides that the firm shall not be automatically dissolved on the death of a partner. The Court emphasized that the reliefs claimed by the plaintiffs, including declaration of co-ownership, representation of the firm, injunctions, and dissolution, cannot be granted in law. The Court referred to precedents holding that if a plaint does not disclose a cause of action or the reliefs sought are not legally tenable, the plaint should be rejected under Order VII Rule 11 CPC to avoid futile litigation and waste of judicial resources. The Court found no merit in the appeals and dismissed them, thereby upholding the rejection of the plaint.

legal_provisions.provision: Order VII Rule 11 of the Civil Procedure Code (CPC)
legal_provisions.relevance: Empowers the court to reject a plaint if it does not disclose a cause of action or the relief claimed is not maintainable. The Court applied this provision to reject the plaint at the threshold as the reliefs sought by the plaintiffs were not legally tenable.

legal_provisions.provision: Sections 40, 42, 43 and 44 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932
legal_provisions.relevance: These sections govern dissolution of a partnership firm by agreement, on contingencies such as death of a partner, by notice, or by the court at the suit of a partner. The Court applied these provisions to hold that only partners can seek dissolution and that the firm is not automatically dissolved on death of a partner as per the partnership deed.

legal_provisions.provision: Clauses 4, 6 and 7 of the Partnership Deed dated 6th December 1943
legal_provisions.relevance: These clauses provide that the partnership shall not be automatically dissolved on death of a partner and that disputes shall be resolved by arbitration, excluding court intervention for dissolution. The Court relied on these clauses to conclude that the plaintiffs cannot claim dissolution or other reliefs.

supporting_paragraphs.text: The partners of a firm are entitled only to the profits of the firm and upon dissolution to the surplus of the sale proceeds of the assets after liabilities. Partners do not have any right, title or interest in the assets while the firm is carrying on business. Hence, the plaintiffs as legal heirs cannot maintain any claim in respect of the assets and properties of the firm.
Only a partner of a firm can seek dissolution of the firm. The plaintiffs are not partners and hence not entitled to claim dissolution or accounts for dissolution.

supporting_paragraphs.paragraph_ref: Paragraphs 23.3 to 23.6 of Dahiben v. Arvindbhai Kalyanji Bhanusali (Gajra) Dead Through Legal Representatives and Others
supporting_paragraphs.text: The power to terminate a civil action under Order VII Rule 11 is drastic and must be strictly adhered to. If a plaint does not disclose a cause of action or is barred by law, the court should reject it to prevent waste of judicial time.
The Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court, after elaborate scrutiny, concluded that the reliefs claimed in the plaint cannot be granted.
The appeals are found to be without merit and are dismissed.
